2023 · ICLR 2023 · Benchmarks & Evals

ManiSkill2: A Unified Benchmark for Generalizable Manipulation Skills

The second generation of the SAPIEN ManiSkill benchmark: 20 manipulation task families spanning rigid- and soft-body, stationary and mobile-base, single- and dual-arm manipulation, with 2000+ object models and 4M+ demonstration frames behind a unified controller/observation interface — plus a render-server architecture built to make visual reinforcement learning fast enough to actually train on all of it.

// the gap

What problem is this solving?

By 2023 there was no shortage of manipulation benchmarks, but each one traded away something the paper's authors considered essential. Home-assistant simulators built for scale — Habitat 2.0 (Szot et al., 2021), ManipulaThor (Ehsani et al., 2021), BEHAVIOR (Srivastava et al., 2022) — mostly use abstract grasp: an object snaps into the gripper when a policy requests it, rather than being physically grasped through contact dynamics. That sidesteps the hardest part of manipulation. Benchmarks with few object-level variations per task — robosuite (Zhu et al., 2020), Meta-World (Yu et al., 2020), RLBench (James et al., 2020) — run a small, fixed roster of objects, so they say little about whether a policy generalizes to object instances it has never seen; of these three, only robosuite and Meta-World actually simulate grasping through contact physics, since the paper's own comparison table (Table 10) classes RLBench's own grasp implementation as abstract, alongside the home-assistant simulators above. And essentially none of them handle soft bodies — clay, liquid, cloth — with the same fully-dynamic rigor: MuJoCo and Bullet's finite-element methods can't handle large deformation or topological change (scooping flour, cutting dough), Flex-based simulators like SoftGym and ThreeDWorld can't realistically model elastoplastic materials like clay, and PlasticineLab (Huang et al., 2021), which does use the material-point method, can't couple its soft bodies to a physically simulated rigid robot.

ManiSkill2 is explicitly framed as "the next generation of the SAPIEN ManiSkill Benchmark (Mu et al., 2021)" — the paper's own predecessor, ManiSkill1 — extending it with fully simulated dynamics, a larger and more varied object set, and large-scale demonstrations. The paper names four specific gaps it is closing: (1) no unified benchmark exists for generic, generalizable manipulation that avoids abstract grasp and thin object variety at once; (2) no benchmark offers real-time, 2-way-coupled rigid-soft-body simulation; (3) benchmarks that do support multiple controllers (action parameterizations) don't let you convert demonstrations collected under one controller into another's action space, which locks large demonstration sets to whatever controller generated them; and (4) Python-based multi-process visual RL environments are throughput- and memory-bound, because each parallel worker process conventionally keeps its own full copy of GPU rendering resources.

// how it works

The method

ManiSkill2 organizes its content into 20 task families — a task family shares an objective but spans many task variants across different assets and initial states, so "PickSingleYCB" is one family covering dozens of object instances, not one fixed scene. The paper groups them into four clusters. Soft-body manipulation (6 families): Fill (pour clay from a bucket into a beaker), Hang (hang a noodle on a rod), Excavate (scoop a target amount of clay to a height), Pour (match a liquid level to a line), Pinch (deform plasticine into a target shape given as an RGBD/point-cloud view from 4 angles), and Write (draw a target character from an alphabet of 50+ on clay, given as a depth map). Precise peg-in-hole assembly (3 families): PegInsertionSide (a cuboid peg into a 3mm-clearance hole — the paper requires half the peg actually inserted, not just proximity), PlugCharger (a dual-peg charger into a 0.5mm-clearance receptacle), and AssemblingKits (fitting shapes into slots carved at any specified clearance, e.g. 0.8mm). For AssemblingKits and PlugCharger, the paper stresses that prior benchmarks' "holes" were visual marks or undefined geometry with nothing to physically insert into; for PegInsertionSide, the upgrade over prior work is the success criterion itself — earlier benchmarks only required the peg head to approach the hole's surface, while ManiSkill2 requires half the peg actually inserted. Stationary 6-DoF pick-and-place (5 families): PickCube, StackCube, PickSingleYCB (YCB objects), PickSingleEGAD (EGAD objects), and PickClutterYCB (picking a specified object out of clutter). Mobile/stationary manipulation of articulated objects (6 families): four inherited directly from ManiSkill1 — PushChair, MoveBucket, OpenCabinetDoor, OpenCabinetDrawer — plus two new ones, TurnFaucet (stationary-arm) and AvoidObstacles (navigating a stationary arm through dense obstacles while sensing the scene). Across all 20 families the paper reports over 2000 object models and over 4M demonstration frames in total — but the mix is uneven by design: e.g. AssemblingKits ships 1,720 demonstration trajectories from 300+ kit configurations and 20 training shapes, PickClutterYCB ships 4,986, and PickSingleYCB ships 100 per object across 74 YCB training objects.

Generalization is built into the task design at the level of held-out object instances, but the paper is not uniform about how it specifies the held-out set. Some splits are fully disclosed: PickSingleEGAD holds out 150 objects from the 1,600-object EGAD training pool (5 demonstration trajectories generated per object); the four mobile-manipulation tasks each hold out exactly 10 unseen cabinets/chairs/buckets from training pools that range 25–42 across the four tasks (25 cabinets for OpenCabinetDrawer, 42 for OpenCabinetDoor, 26 chairs, 29 buckets); TurnFaucet holds out 18 faucet models against 60 training models. Others are looser: PickSingleYCB and PickClutterYCB's test objects are described only as "another confidential set of 40 objects from other sources," without naming what that set is. "Generalizable" in this paper's title and abstract refers specifically to generalizing across object instances within a task family — not across task families, not across robots. The three fixed-geometry families vary what they reshuffle per episode differently: PlugCharger uses one fixed charger/receptacle geometry and randomizes only initial poses; PegInsertionSide additionally randomizes the hole's position and size, not just poses; and AvoidObstacles randomizes the shape and layout of the obstacles themselves, not merely the arm's starting pose.

Two systems contributions do the load-bearing engineering work. First, multi-controller conversion: ManiSkill2 lets you record demonstrations under one controller (e.g. the joint-position controller used to generate them via task-and-motion planning) and replay them under a different target controller (e.g. delta end-effector pose, used for imitation/reinforcement learning), while reproducing the same underlying dynamics. The conversion is closed-loop: the desired target-frame pose is recovered via forward kinematics from the source action, then combined with the *target* environment's current pose (not the source's), so execution errors don't accumulate the way an open-loop conversion's would:

atgt(t) = T̄tgt(t) · Ttgt-1(t) = T̄src(t) · Ttgt-1(t) = FK(āsrc(t)) · Ttgt-1(t) // a target-controller action recovered from a source-controller demonstration; T̄=desired pose, T=current pose, FK=forward kinematics

Second, asynchronous rendering plus a render server. In a conventional multi-process visual-RL pipeline, each worker simulates physics, renders its own images on its own copy of GPU resources, waits for the GPU, then copies images CPU→GPU→CPU→GPU again on the way to the policy network — and the CPU sits idle during the wait. ManiSkill2 overlaps reward computation with the render wait ("asynchronous rendering"), and additionally offers a render server: a thread pool on the main process that services every worker's render requests from one shared set of GPU meshes and textures, eliminating the GPU→CPU→GPU round trip and letting memory be shared instead of duplicated per process.

Alongside this, the soft-body simulator is a custom 2-way-coupled rigid–MPM (material point method) engine built on Nvidia's Warp JIT framework — the paper states it is, to the authors' knowledge, the first embodied-AI environment to support real-time 2-way-coupled rigid-MPM simulation, letting a physically simulated robot arm push, scoop, and deform clay, liquid, and dough while those materials in turn exert force back on the arm.

// what they found

The results

The throughput headline needs care about which number is which. The abstract states "a CNN-based policy can collect samples at about 2000 FPS with 1 GPU and 16 processes"; the introduction restates it as "an RGBD-input PPO policy at about 2000 FPS ... with 1 GPU and 16 CPU processors." Both are describing the same point on the render-server curve at 16 parallel environments — a separate number from Table 1(a)'s reported peak. That table, run on PickCube with 16 CPU cores of an Intel i9-9960X, 128GB RAM, and one RTX Titan (24GB), sweeps 16/32/.../512 parallel environments and reports each framework's best point: ManiSkill2 with the render server ("ManiSkill2-Server") peaks at 2487±24 FPS (random actions) / 2532±63 FPS (Nature-CNN policy) at 64 environments — nearly double Habitat 2.0's peak of 1275±10 FPS (also at 64 envs), and roughly 2.7–2.9× RoboSuite 1.3's 924±3 FPS (at 32 envs) and Isaac Gym's 865±35 FPS (at 512 envs, i.e. Isaac Gym needed 8× the parallelism to reach only about a third — 865/2487 ≈ 0.35 — of ManiSkill2-Server's throughput). Table 1's third configuration, labeled "ManiSkill2-Sync," is not the async-without-server case; it is ManiSkill2 run fully synchronously (neither asynchronous rendering nor a render server), and it manages only 942±19 / 931±4 FPS — barely ahead of RoboSuite, behind Habitat. The async-without-server configuration is a separate curve in Figure 3 (there labeled plain "ManiSkill2," and not reported in Table 1 at all): the paper states that this configuration alone "is already able to outperform the speed of other frameworks," peaking near 1800 FPS in Figure 3 — so asynchronous rendering by itself accounts for most of the gap over Habitat/RoboSuite/Isaac Gym, with the render server adding the further push from there up to the 2487–2532 FPS peak.

Memory tells a similar story with one disclosed asymmetry: extending PickClutterYCB to 74 YCB objects per scene, ManiSkill2-Server holds steady at 4.9G→5.1G→5.8G GPU memory as parallel environments go from 4→8→64, while Habitat 2.0 grows from 6.4G→12.9G→out-of-memory over the same range. The paper is explicit that this test "enable[s] GPU texture compression for Habitat and use[s] regular textures for ManiSkill2" — i.e. the comparison already gives Habitat an advantage it isn't using elsewhere in the paper, which makes the still-much-larger Habitat growth curve more notable, not less, but also means the raw 2.5×-at-8-envs gap isn't an apples-to-apples texture-format comparison.

On policy learning, imitation learning (behavior cloning, 50k gradient steps) is weak almost everywhere except the two easiest soft-body tasks: from Table 2, point-cloud BC gets 0.45±0.04 on Fill and 0.35±0.15 on Hang, but only 0.08±0.04 on Excavate, 0.02±0.02 on Pour, and 0.00±0.00 on both Pinch and Write; on rigid tasks it manages 0.22±0.06 on PickCube and 0.04±0.02 on StackCube, with every rigid assembly task (PegInsertionSide, PlugCharger, AssemblingKits) at 0 (not shown in the table). Point cloud does not uniformly beat RGBD here, either: RGBD actually wins on Fill (0.62±0.07 vs 0.45±0.04) and Excavate (0.21±0.04 vs 0.08±0.04) — the opposite of the pattern on rigid tasks, where point cloud is ahead or tied everywhere in Table 3.

Demonstration-augmented RL (DAPG+PPO, 25M timesteps, Table 3) does much better on pick-and-place — 0.94±0.03 (PickCube), 0.95±0.02 (StackCube), 0.51±0.05 (PickSingleYCB), all point cloud — but is still near zero on every high-precision task: PegInsertionSide 0.01±0.01, PlugCharger 0.01±0.02, AssemblingKits 0.00±0.00, TurnFaucet 0.04±0.03, AvoidObstacles 0.00±0.00. Swapping the delta end-effector pose controller for a delta joint-position controller on PickSingleYCB — same point-cloud agent, same task — drops success from 0.51±0.05 to 0.22±0.18, which the paper reads as evidence for how much the controller choice itself matters. On held-out test objects (Table 6, Appendix F.4), PickSingleYCB's point-cloud success falls from 0.51±0.05 (training objects) to 0.36±0.06 (held-out); RGBD falls from 0.18±0.07 to 0.08±0.03. AssemblingKits and AvoidObstacles stay flat at 0.00±0.00 in both tables — there's no success left to lose — but TurnFaucet does slip further, from 0.04±0.03/0.03±0.03 (point cloud/RGBD, training objects) to 0.01±0.01/0.01±0.01 (held-out): too small a drop to read as a meaningful generalization signal, but not "no further degradation."

Sense-plan-act baselines are reported for two tasks only. Contact-GraspNet (a pretrained grasp-pose predictor) combined with motion planning reaches 43.24% success on PickSingleYCB (5 trials × 74 objects); the paper attributes failures to low-confidence predicted poses (27.03% of trials, concentrated on small/thin objects like spoons and forks) and to high-confidence poses that are nonetheless low-quality or kinematically unreachable (29.73%). Transporter Networks on AssemblingKits reach 18% success under ManiSkill2's own strict criterion — the piece must actually fit into the hole — versus 99% under the original Transporter Networks pose-accuracy criterion (peg within 1cm/15° of the goal pose), even after the paper increased the model's rotation-prediction resolution from 36 to 144 bins to help it. Finally, a sim-to-real check on PickCube: a point-cloud policy trained for 10M steps reaches 91.0% success in simulation and 60.0% over 50 real-world trials with a ROKAE xMate3Pro arm and an Intel RealSense D415.

// does it hold up?

The eval read

The systems comparison is honest where it's hardest to be: the paper's own footnote admits "a fair comparison of different frameworks is still challenging as their simulation and rendering differ in fidelity," and Appendix E.3 discloses that the collision meshes used for timing differ in complexity across simulators (1,009 vertices for ManiSkill2/Habitat 2.0 vs 1,210 for Isaac Gym/RoboSuite, though visual meshes match at 69,747 vertices for all four) and that the memory test gives Habitat GPU texture compression ManiSkill2 doesn't use. Those are real caveats to the FPS and memory numbers, but they're the paper's own disclosures, not something a reader has to dig for — and they cut in a specific direction: fixing them would likely widen ManiSkill2's memory lead (removing Habitat's compression advantage) while leaving the mesh-complexity asymmetry's effect on FPS unresolved either way.

Two things are less well specified. First, the held-out object sets that back the paper's central "generalizable" claim are inconsistently documented: EGAD's 150-object holdout, the mobile-manipulation tasks' 10-unseen-instance holdouts, and TurnFaucet's 18-object holdout are all precisely stated, but PickSingleYCB and PickClutterYCB — two of the paper's core pick-and-place tasks — hold out against "another confidential set of 40 objects from other sources" that is never named. A reader can't audit what that test distribution actually contains or how far it sits from the YCB training objects. Second, six of the 20 task families carry zero reported success-rate evidence anywhere in this paper. Four — PushChair, MoveBucket, OpenCabinetDoor, OpenCabinetDrawer, all inherited unchanged from ManiSkill1 — are fully specified in Appendix C.6 (objective, success metric, demonstration count, evaluation protocol) but are never run through any baseline: not behavior cloning, not DAPG+PPO, not sense-plan-act. Two more, PickSingleEGAD and PickClutterYCB, are fully specified in Appendix C.2 and are mentioned elsewhere — PickClutterYCB only as the subject of the GPU-memory scaling test in Table 1(b), which reports memory, not success, and PickSingleEGAD only in Table 10's domain-randomization footnote — but neither has a results row in any table either. Tables 2, 3, 6, 7, and 8 and Appendices F.1–F.8 cover only the other 14 families. That leaves 6 of 20 task families (30%) with zero reported success-rate evidence in ManiSkill2 itself, even though the assets and demonstrations of all 20 are counted toward its claimed scope in the paper's own comparison table (Table 10).

The reported baselines are appropriate for a 2023 systems paper — one classical sense-plan-act pipeline per task type (Contact-GraspNet, Transporter Networks), plus behavior cloning and demonstration-augmented PPO as the learning baselines — but that is also a narrow slice: no policy achieves non-trivial success on any of the three precision-assembly tasks under default clearances, and Appendix F.7's own ablation (loosening clearance 10× on PegInsertionSide) shows point-cloud DAPG+PPO jumping from 0.01±0.01 to 0.74±0.10 — evidence that at least part of the difficulty is the clearance dial itself rather than an intrinsic ceiling on the algorithms tested, but PlugCharger stays low (0.02±0.02 point cloud, 0.29±0.07 RGBD) even at 10× clearance, so the two assembly tasks don't fail for identical reasons.

baselines

Reasonable and disclosed for a systems benchmark of this scope (one SPA pipeline per applicable task type, BC and DAPG+PPO for IL/RL), but six of 20 task families have no baseline run at all, and the SPA comparisons cover only 2 of 20 families.

contamination

Not an LLM-style leakage risk, but the analogous concern — how "unseen" the held-out object split really is — is fully specified for some tasks (EGAD, mobile manipulation, TurnFaucet) and left as an unnamed "confidential set of 40 objects" for PickSingleYCB/PickClutterYCB.

what's missed

The 2000+ FPS headline is measured on PickCube alone — the simplest rigid task, no soft-body or clutter active — so it characterizes the render server, not runtime on the benchmark's own soft-body or dense-clutter tasks.

would raise confidence

Any success-rate baseline (even a weak one) on the six un-benchmarked task families (the four mobile-manipulation tasks, PickSingleEGAD, and PickClutterYCB), and a named/described version of the confidential 40-object YCB/clutter test set.

// bottom line

ManiSkill2's systems engineering claims hold up under its own scrutiny — the render-server throughput and memory numbers are measured against real competing frameworks with disclosed, direction-known caveats. Its benchmark-scope claims hold up less evenly: the paper reports meaningful evidence of a generalization gap where it measures one (PickSingleYCB's 0.51→0.36 point-cloud drop to held-out objects), but 6 of its 20 task families (30%) ship with no baseline evidence at all, and its most-used pick-and-place holdout set is never named.

// takeaways

What to remember

  1. ManiSkill2 packages 20 manipulation task families — soft-body, precision assembly, pick-and-place, and mobile/articulated-object manipulation — behind one controller-conversion interface, with over 2000 object models and over 4M demonstration frames total, but the mix per family is uneven by design — e.g. 1,720 AssemblingKits trajectories vs. 4,986 PickClutterYCB trajectories.
  2. The "2000 FPS" headline (16 parallel environments) and Table 1's reported peak (2487–2532 FPS at 64 environments) are two different points on the same render-server curve, not the same number restated — both are real, but conflating them overstates or understates the comparison depending on which one gets quoted against a competing framework's own peak.
  3. "Generalizable" in this paper means generalizing across held-out object instances within a task family, with that holdout precisely specified for some families (EGAD, mobile manipulation, TurnFaucet) and left as an unnamed confidential set for two of its core pick-and-place families (PickSingleYCB, PickClutterYCB) — and six task families (the four inherited from ManiSkill1, plus PickSingleEGAD and PickClutterYCB) carry no baseline results in this paper at all.
